newsitem.title: SYRIA: Chirac's call for EU role divides Middle East.
newsitem.headline: Chirac's call for EU role divides Middle East.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac's call for the European Union to co-sponsor Arab-Israeli peace talks divided the Middle East along predictable lines on Sunday, with Syria applauding and Israel objecting.

In a speech in Damascus on the first leg of a six-stop tour of the region, Chirac said on Saturday night that the peace process was in danger and Europe must play a greater role, contributing proposals and not just money.

"France and Europe must stand by the parties as sources of friendship and proposals, and not as mere partners for reconstruction. It is time for Europe to co-sponsor this process as well," he said at a dinner with President Hafez al-Assad.
The Syrian leader endorsed his call, while saying Europe was no substitute for U.S. mediation.

"I do not see any contradiction between a European role and the efforts which the United States has made and is still making, as long as all are pushing the peace process forward," Assad said in a toast punctuated by an embarrassed silence when he lost his place and fumbled for a long moment with his text.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy rejected the French call even before Chirac sets foot in the Jewish state on Monday.
"A mediator entering into the conflict -- or into the negotiations -- is inconceivable," Levy said. "Every (outside) force that will enter into the negotiations puts obstacles into the negotiations."

French officials said Chirac was not demanding that the EU sit in on the negotiations. But the current negotiating system had shown its limits since the new Israeli goverment had sought to go back on understandings reached by its predecessor and the Arabs felt the United States was unbalanced, they said.

As an example of a possible Middle East role, a French official cited the way French and EU diplomacy had complemented U.S. negotiating efforts in Bosnia, most recently by proposing a two-year stabilisation period to consolidate peace there.

The official said Israeli and U.S. opposition did not make such a role easy and he acknowledged not all in the EU shared France's activism. Britain was loathe to offend Washington and Germany had a historic complex in dealing with Israel.
But he predicted that in the long run even Israel would see that the EU's economic weight and good ties with countries such as Syria or Iran could advance peace.
Chirac's efforts to tread a delicate line between France's Arab policy and its need to show friendship and understanding for Israel have caused two other clashes before he arrives.

After Israel objected to his plan to send Foreign Minister Herve de Charette to a disputed PLO headquarters in Arab East Jerusalem, he dropped de Charette from the Israel leg of his trip and will send a junior minister to Orient House instead.

A visit to the Israeli parliament was hastily added to his programme on Sunday after Knesset Speaker Dan Tichon threatened to boycott his speech in the city of Haifa on Monday, noting he planned to address the Palestinian and Jordanian parliaments.
Beyond these diplomatic incidents, the French leader has already seen a wide gulf separating right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from his Arab partners.

Assad said Syria would produce proof that Israel's previous Labour government had gone beyond talk in making commitments to hand back the occupied Golan Heights in negotiations near Washington, suspended earlier this year.
The French official said Assad did not claim to Chirac that there was a signed or sealed agreement, but he had referred to assurances conveyed via the United States.
Chirac and Assad held a second round of talks on Sunday, due to focus on details of the peace process and Lebanon, and were to hold a joint news conference later.
